text: Before you go, listen to this. It's music by Johann Sebastian Bach, played on a cello. A cello has four strings. A player presses a string to make the part that plays shorter, and a shorter part sings a higher note. Just like Pythagoras's string. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn how to name a fraction. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try one on your own. Let's begin.
Now it's your turn to work on your own. Use what you learned: equal parts, how many, and of what. You've got this.
These three jobs each have a mix-up that kids often make with fractions. Your job is to find it and fix it. Take your time, and look closely at every part.
Last stop! Show what you know. Remember: a fraction needs equal parts. The bottom number tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number tells how many parts you're counting.

This is a string over a wooden box, like the one in the stories. First, pluck the whole string and listen. Then slide the two bridges to cut the string into 3 parts. Here's a secret: parts that are the same length sing the same note. Use your ears and your eyes.
You did it! Three parts, all the same length, so they all sing the same note. Each part is one of 3 equal parts. In math, we call that one-third. Hold on to that idea. We'll use it all lesson long.

Hoo, hello! I'm Opti. Come sit with me and open this old book. Each chapter visits a real time and place where people used math. Today's chapter is Ancient Greece, more than 2,500 years ago. Meet Pythagoras. He loved numbers, and he loved music. Stories say he stretched one string over a long wooden box. Then he listened very carefully. Let's listen too.

Before you go, listen to Bach's music on the cello again. A cello player presses each string at just the right spot. The same spot on the string always makes the same note, just like a fraction always lands on the same spot on a number line. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn how to draw a number line and put a fraction on it. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try it on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. This number line keeps going past 1. Count the jumps carefully. Each jump is one unit fraction.
Each of these jobs has a mix-up that kids often make on a number line. Find it and fix it. Count the spaces, not just the marks.
Last stop! Show what you know. Cut the line into equal parts. Count the jumps from 0. Then label the spot.
The string is cut into 5 equal parts. Let's count them out loud together. Tap each bridge, from left to right, and say its name with me. One-fifth. Two-fifths. Keep going, all the way to the end.
Listen to that! Five-fifths is the whole string. Five-fifths is 1. The start of the string is 0, and the end is 1. Each bridge left a tick mark. Our string just became a number line.

Hoo, welcome back! Let's open our old book to the same chapter. We're still in Ancient Greece with Pythagoras and his singing string. Last time, we cut the string into equal parts. Today, the string turns into something new: a number line. Every fraction gets its very own spot.

Before you go, listen to Bach's music on the cello one more time. Listen for the low notes and the high notes. Long parts of a string sing low, and short parts sing high, just like our fractions today. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.

Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn how to compare two fractions with the same denominator and write the answer with a symbol. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try it on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. On a number line, the fraction farther to the right is greater. Count the jumps from 0 to find each spot.
Each of these jobs has a mix-up that kids often make when they compare fractions. Find it and fix it. Remember: the open side of the symbol always faces the greater fraction.
Last stop! Show what you know. Check that the wholes are the same. Count the equal parts. Then write your answer with a symbol.
Both strings are cut into ninths, so every part is the same size. Slide one bridge to four-ninths and the other bridge to seven-ninths. Then pluck both parts and listen. Which part is longer?
Did you hear it? The longer part sings a lower note. Seven-ninths is more string than four-ninths, because seven parts are more than four parts of the same size. Seven-ninths is greater.

Hoo, welcome back to Chapter 9! Pythagoras now has two strings, side by side. Both strings are the same length, and both are cut into the same number of equal parts. Today, we'll find out which fraction is greater, and we'll even hear the answer.

Before you go, listen to some organ music by Bach. An organ has hundreds of pipes. The long pipes play the low notes, and the short pipes play the high notes. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn how to compare fractions that have the same numerator. Next, we fix some mix-ups together and play a tune. Then you try it on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. On two number lines of the same length, count the jumps. Then look at how long each jump is.
Each of these jobs has a mix-up that kids often make. Here's a clue: a bigger denominator does not make a bigger fraction. It means the whole is cut into more pieces, so each piece is smaller.
Last stop! Show what you know. When the numerators match, look at the denominators. Fewer pieces in the whole means bigger pieces.
Both pipes are the same length. Cut the top pipe into nine equal pieces and the bottom pipe into twelve. Then blow one piece of each and listen. Which piece is longer?
Did you hear it? The one-twelfth piece whistled higher, because it is shorter. When you cut the same pipe into more pieces, each piece gets smaller. So one-ninth is greater than one-twelfth.
